summary.title: ATTACK-Navi
summary.description: STRIDE threat model of ATTACK-Navi, a browser-based MITRE ATT&CK workbench served as a static site, with an optional proxy that holds OpenCTI and MISP credentials. Elements, flows and threats were derived from the code on main; each threat's description cites the relevant files.

data.name: Analyst (browser user)
data.description: Person using the workbench. Types integration credentials (MISP API key, OpenCTI token, TAXII username and password, NVD API key), imports layer, STIX and workspace files, and opens share links whose #import= fragment carries a base64 STIX bundle. Every integration URL and credential is entered here, and no scheme or host is validated: saveConfig only trims a trailing slash.

threats.title: Share-link #import= bundle can attach attacker-written notes to built-in ATT&CK techniques
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: A share link carries a base64 STIX bundle in #import=. The collection panel parses it on load and shows a confirm dialog with object counts only. On confirm, importCollection records attackIds even for skipped attack-patterns. Each STIX note whose object_refs resolve to one of those IDs is written with annotationSvc.setAnnotation, which replaces the existing note for that technique. A link that looks harmless ('1 technique, 1 note') can therefore overwrite real analyst notes on techniques such as T1059 with attacker-chosen text. The Navigator-layer importer explicitly avoids this ('imports never clobber existing analyst work'); this importer does not. On main (#125) importCollection keeps an existing note instead of replacing it and reports the conflict, and both confirm dialogs name the techniques whose notes would conflict. Evidence on main: src/app/services/stix-collection.service.ts:191-197 (skipped IDs still mapped), :287-306 (an existing note is kept and reported; setAnnotation only when the technique has none), :397-418 (hash parse; preview from summarizeBundle); src/app/services/annotation.service.ts:24-37 (map.set replaces); src/app/components/collection-panel/collection-panel.component.ts:173-192 (confirm dialog, then importCollection); src/app/components/collection-panel/collection-panel.component.html:332-354 (dialog names conflicting technique IDs at :345-350); src/app/services/navigator-layer.service.ts:219-220 (the same never-clobber rule)
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main (#125): existing annotations are skipped on import, as navigator-layer.service does, and the confirm dialog names the technique IDs whose notes conflict. Remaining: an imported note still lands on any built-in ATT&CK ID that has no note yet; treat imported notes as custom-entity notes rather than notes on built-in ATT&CK IDs.

data.name: Analyst browser origin sandbox
data.description: Everything that runs in, or is stored for, the SPA's origin: the Angular app, the service worker, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and Cache Storage. On GitHub Pages the origin is https://teamstarwolf.github.io, which every TeamStarWolf project page shares, and no CSP is served there. Self-hosted, it is the nginx origin with a strict CSP (nginx-security-headers.conf:14, rendered into the nginx config at container start). Any script running in the origin can read all of these stores.

data.name: Angular SPA (browser)
data.description: The Angular 22 workbench running in the analyst's browser tab, with hash routing and an XHR HttpClient. No HTTP interceptor is registered (src/app/app.config.ts:19), so no header is added globally; proxy-mode OpenCTI and MISP calls add X-Requested-With and, when the analyst has entered one, the proxy access token as X-Proxy-Key (src/app/services/proxy-headers.ts:15-19). The SPA parses STIX from upstream, from TAXII, from file imports and from #import= links. ATT&CK description text is rendered through the attackText pipe, which reduces input to plain text with DOMParser, HTML-escapes it, and binds through [innerHTML] under Angular's sanitizer with no trust bypass. The only bypassSecurityTrustHtml call left is for static icon SVGs.

threats.title: Stored/DOM XSS from upstream or imported description text rendered with [innerHTML]
threats.description: The sidebar binds technique, detection, procedure, relationship and mitigation descriptions with [innerHTML]. These come from live upstream STIX, TAXII collections, share links, and custom or imported entities. A trust bypass in this path would give script execution in a credential-holding origin. Evidence: src/app/pipes/attack-text.pipe.ts:9-17, :20-56; src/app/components/sidebar/sidebar.component.html:112, :389, :422, :449, :1744, :1753; src/app/shared/icons/icon.component.ts:41-50
threats.mitigation: AttackTextPipe reduces input to text with DOMParser and HTML-escapes everything. It then re-adds only anchors it builds itself from [label](https?://...) markdown, with a URL character class that excludes quotes, angle brackets and whitespace. It returns a plain string and no longer calls bypassSecurityTrustHtml, so Angular's sanitizer still runs on binding. The only remaining bypassSecurityTrustHtml call is in IconComponent, on compile-time constant SVG from the icon registry, with unknown names mapped to a fallback.

data.name: Angular service worker (ngsw)
data.description: PWA service worker, registered only in production builds and scoped to the base href. Stale registrations at other scopes are removed. It intercepts same-origin and listed cross-origin GETs and serves them with a freshness strategy. When the network takes longer than 10-15 s it returns cached upstream STIX, mapping content and NVD/EPSS responses, up to 6-24 h old.

threats.title: Service worker serves cached app-shell code without re-verifying hashes, so one cache write gives persistent code execution
threats.description: ngsw-config.json prefetches index.html and the main and polyfills bundles into Cache Storage. The Angular worker checks content against the ngsw.json hash only when it fetches from the network. Once a hashed URL is in the cache, the cached response is returned without any check. Any same-origin script can overwrite the ngsw:/ATTACK-Navi/ app-shell cache entry for main-*.js with its own code, and that code then runs on every later visit, including offline, until the next app version is deployed. The script could come from a sibling github.io site or a one-time XSS. A `javascript:` reference URL in STIX data is not such a source on main (#132): DataService keeps only http(s) reference URLs and falls back to the canonical ATT&CK page (src/app/services/data.service.ts:949-968), and the HTML report emits only http(s) hrefs (src/app/services/html-report.service.ts:34-42). This turns a transient compromise into a persistent one in an origin that handles OpenCTI, MISP and TAXII credentials. Evidence: ngsw-config.json:5-10 (app-shell prefetch); node_modules/@angular/service-worker/ngsw-worker.js:426-434 (@angular/service-worker 22.2.2 per package-lock.json) (cached hashed response returned as-is), :562-578 (hash checked only on network fetch); src/main.ts:46-48 (registration)
threats.mitigation: Remove the shared-origin exposure (dedicated origin). Ship a strict CSP so one-time injection is harder. Consider an app-level integrity check that compares loaded bundle hashes against a server-fetched ngsw.json, or skip the service worker on the shared-origin Pages deployment. Document an 'Unregister SW and clear site data' recovery step.

data.name: Browser localStorage
data.description: Plaintext per-origin persistent storage, 37 localStorage.setItem call sites outside the specs. Holds settings (with the NVD key stripped), org name and base64 logo, layers, annotations, tags, watchlists, and integration config: MISP and OpenCTI URL, mode and proxyUrl, plus the TAXII server list with usernames (passwords stripped). On the shared github.io origin, any script running there can read it, and so can any XSS.

threats.title: Shared teamstarwolf.github.io origin exposes all browser storage to sibling Pages sites
threats.description: The app is published at https://teamstarwolf.github.io/ATTACK-Navi/. localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and Cache Storage are scoped to the origin, not the path, so every other Pages project under teamstarwolf.github.io can read and write them, as can an XSS in any of those projects. Exposed data: asset inventory, emulation plans, implementation status, MISP/OpenCTI server and proxy URLs, TAXII server URLs and usernames, the STIX cache, and user layers. sessionStorage, which holds the NVD key and, on main, the proxy access token, also carries over when the same tab navigates to a sibling path. The app itself shows the cross-app reach: on every load, main.ts unregisters every service worker on the origin whose scope is not ATTACK-Navi's base path, which removes other TeamStarWolf PWAs' offline support. Evidence: package.json:5 (homepage teamstarwolf.github.io/ATTACK-Navi/); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:36; src/main.ts:24-37 (unregisters all other registrations), :40-50; src/app/services/asset-inventory.service.ts:536; src/app/services/emulation-plan.service.ts:413; src/app/services/misp.service.ts:150-155; src/app/services/opencti.service.ts:161-165; src/app/services/taxii.service.ts:198-202; src/app/services/data.service.ts:53-54; src/app/services/user-layer.service.ts:19-20,465; src/app/services/settings.service.ts:192, :197
threats.mitigation: Serve the hosted app from a dedicated origin, such as a custom domain via a CNAME in public/, or a separate github.io account used only for this site. Limit cleanupStaleServiceWorkers to registrations whose script URL is this app's ngsw-worker.js. Consider encrypting sensitive work product at rest, with a key held in memory only.

threats.title: Integration credentials persisted to localStorage or leaked through workspace bundles
threats.description: The analyst enters an OpenCTI token, a MISP API key, TAXII passwords and an NVD key in Settings, and on main (#114) a proxy access token. If any of these were written to localStorage, or included in the shareable workspace export, they would end up on disk and in files handed to teammates. Evidence: src/app/services/misp.service.ts:118-136, :149-155; src/app/services/opencti.service.ts:131-148, :160-165; src/app/services/taxii.service.ts:198-203; src/app/services/settings.service.ts:158-183, :185-201; src/app/services/workspace-bundle.service.ts:15-18, :23-54 (taxii key at :46), :94-101, :115-124
threats.mitigation: MISP and OpenCTI save only the URL, mode and proxy URL, and set apiKey and token to '' on load. TAXII strips the password before saving. The NVD key is removed from the localStorage settings and kept in sessionStorage. The proxy access token is handled the same way (stripped from the localStorage settings and kept in sessionStorage only, src/app/services/settings.service.ts:189-200, as README.md:201 documents), so like the NVD key it is readable by any same-origin script. The workspace bundle allowlist excludes misp_config and opencti_config, strips nvdApiKey on both export and import, and rejects keys that are not on the allowlist. Outside this threat: server URLs, TAXII usernames and proxy URLs are identifiers rather than secrets, and are still stored in plaintext and exported (mitre-nav-taxii-v1, src/app/services/workspace-bundle.service.ts:46); the NVD key's separate path to disk through the service-worker cache is tracked as e4c3c3f7.

data.name: Browser sessionStorage
data.description: Tab-session storage that holds the NVD API key under 'mitre-nav-settings-v1-key' and the proxy access token under 'mitre-nav-settings-v1-proxy-token' (src/app/services/settings.service.ts:189-200). It survives a reload but not closing the tab or browser, and any script on the origin can read it.

data.name: IndexedDB (STIX cache + user layers)
data.description: Two databases. 'mitre-navigator-cache/stix-bundles' holds raw upstream STIX bundles with a timestamp; within the 24 h TTL they are re-parsed and trusted on load, with no signature or hash check. 'attack-navi-user-layers/layers' holds the analyst's saved layers.

data.name: Service-worker Cache Storage
data.description: Cache Storage managed by ngsw. It holds the prefetched app shell and lazy JS and assets, plus freshness dataGroups: mitre-attack STIX (24 h, 10 entries), external content from CTID, Red Canary, Sigma, Elastic, Splunk, MISP and mitre/cti (12 h, 20 entries), and api.first.org and NVD responses (6 h, 50 entries). The NVD key travels in a header rather than the URL, so the cached data is response bodies only.

threats.title: NVD API key can persist in the service-worker cache, contrary to the sessionStorage design
threats.description: SettingsService keeps the NVD key out of localStorage. Its comment says the key lives in sessionStorage and 'never persists to disk'. The key itself is never written to localStorage or to a file by the app: CveService sends it only as an 'apiKey' request header on GETs to services.nvd.nist.gov. The exposure is indirect: that host is in the ngsw 'apis' data group (freshness strategy), and the Angular worker caches each successful response with cache.put(req, res.clone()), passing the original Request. The Cache API stores a request together with its headers (they are needed for Vary matching), so the apiKey header can land in persistent Cache Storage, outlive the browser session, and be read by any same-origin script through caches.open(...).keys(). How much of the stored request a browser keeps on disk is implementation-defined; confirm in the target browser before changing the status. Evidence: src/app/services/settings.service.ts:185-201 (comment at :187-188); src/app/services/cve.service.ts:339, :354-355; ngsw-config.json:58-66; node_modules/@angular/service-worker/ngsw-worker.js:1029-1040 (DataGroup.cacheResponse, `put(req, res.clone())` at :1040; @angular/service-worker 22.2.2 per package-lock.json)
threats.mitigation: Remove services.nvd.nist.gov from the ngsw 'apis' data group, or send NVD requests with the ngsw-bypass header so the worker does not cache them. Clear the existing ngsw:*:data:apis caches when the key changes or is removed.

data.name: Operator host / user's local network
data.description: The analyst's or operator's machine and LAN, where the optional Express proxy and its server/.env secrets live. docker-compose publishes the proxy on 127.0.0.1:8787 only (docker-compose.yml:24-25), and the browser also reaches it same-origin through the app's nginx /api/ route on 8080 (all interfaces); because the compose proxy binds 0.0.0.0 (:43-44) it answers 503 on every route except /api/health until PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN is set, and its Host allowlist admits only loopback names unless APP_HOST is set (:41-42). `npm run proxy:start` binds 127.0.0.1 unless HOST is set (server/src/index.js:18), a non-loopback HOST without PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN answers 503 on every route except /api/health, and the SPA can send the token as X-Proxy-Key (README.md:201-203). User MISP, OpenCTI and TAXII servers may also sit on this network.

data.name: Optional Express credential proxy
data.description: A Node/Express service on port 8787 that holds the OpenCTI and MISP secrets so the browser never sees them. It binds 127.0.0.1 unless HOST is set (server/src/index.js:18, :420-427); docker-compose sets HOST=0.0.0.0 in the container, publishes it on 127.0.0.1:8787 and puts it behind nginx's same-origin /api/ route (docker-compose.yml:24-25, :44). Before any upstream call, every /api/* route except /api/health checks the Host name against loopback names plus ALLOWED_HOSTS, then checks PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN (Bearer or X-Proxy-Key) when it is set, or answers 503 on a non-loopback bind without it, then requires X-Requested-With (server/src/index.js:306). The SPA sends the token when the analyst enters it. CORS admits an origin allowlist, and requests with no Origin header are allowed (server/src/index.js:27-47). OpenCTI GraphQL is forwarded only for allowlisted root fields, MISP only for a read-only endpoint allowlist, and upstream paths are pinned to the configured origin. Responses are relayed with the upstream status and Content-Type, bounded by a timeout and a size cap (server/src/index.js:177-196).

threats.title: Unauthenticated callers on the network can use the proxy's OpenCTI and MISP credentials
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: Caller authentication only runs when PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN is set (requireProxyToken returns next() otherwise). The shipped `.env.example` leaves it empty. The SPA's proxy mode never sends `Authorization` or `X-Proxy-Key`, so an operator who sets the token breaks the app. In practice the token stays empty. `app.listen(port)` passes no host, so `npm run proxy:start` binds every interface, while the startup log and the code comment say it is localhost-only. Any host on the same network can then call POST /api/opencti/graphql and GET/POST /api/misp/* with no Origin header, which CORS lets through. Each call carries the operator's OPENCTI_TOKEN or MISP_API_KEY upstream. On main (#114) the proxy binds 127.0.0.1 unless HOST is set, answers 503 on every route except /api/health when HOST is not loopback and PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN is unset, compares the token in constant time, and the SPA sends it as X-Proxy-Key; with the token unset on a loopback bind, any local process can still call the proxy. Evidence on main: server/src/index.js:89-103 (token enforced when set; when unset, served only on a loopback bind, 503 otherwise); server/src/index.js:81-87 (timingSafeEqual compare); server/src/index.js:37 (requests with no Origin header are still allowed by CORS); server/src/index.js:420-427 (listen on HOST, which defaults to 127.0.0.1 at :18; the log prints the real bind address); server/.env.example:26 (PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN still empty by default); src/app/services/opencti.service.ts:351-352 and src/app/services/misp.service.ts:311-316 (proxy mode sends X-Requested-With and, when set, X-Proxy-Key); README.md:201-203 (proxy access token field in Settings, loopback bind, fail-closed non-loopback HOST)
threats.mitigation: docker-compose publishes the proxy on 127.0.0.1:8787 only (docker-compose.yml:24-25), and the browser also reaches it same-origin through the app's nginx /api/ route on 8080 (all interfaces); because the compose proxy binds 0.0.0.0 (:43-44) it answers 503 on every route except /api/health until PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN is set, and its Host allowlist admits only loopback names unless APP_HOST is set (:41-42). Implemented on main (#114): the default bind is 127.0.0.1 (`app.listen(port, host)` with HOST defaulting to loopback, server/src/index.js:18, :420-427); Settings > Integrations has a "Proxy access token" field whose value opencti.service.ts and misp.service.ts send as `X-Proxy-Key` (src/app/services/proxy-headers.ts:15-19), kept in sessionStorage only like the NVD key (src/app/services/settings.service.ts:189-200); a non-loopback HOST without PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN starts but refuses every route except /api/health with 503, rather than refusing to start (server/src/index.js:66-73, :89-94); tokens are compared with crypto.timingSafeEqual (server/src/index.js:81-87). Accepted rather than open: with the token unset on a loopback bind, any process on the same host can call the proxy. That is the documented single-user default: the proxy prints a warning at start (server/src/index.js:74-78), server/.env.example:21-26 says to leave the token unset only for isolated localhost use and to set it whenever the proxy is reachable beyond 127.0.0.1, and a browser page on that host is still held off by the Host allowlist, the X-Requested-With requirement and CORS (server/src/index.js:113-145, :306; threats ac3cd11c and 1ced7e5e).

threats.title: A proxy caller can run arbitrary OpenCTI GraphQL, including mutations, with the operator's token
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: MISP gets a read-only endpoint allowlist, but /api/opencti/graphql only checks that `query` is a string and `variables` is an object. It then forwards both under `Authorization: Bearer ${OPENCTI_TOKEN}`. Any caller that gets past the weak gate (an unauthenticated LAN host, a script on an allowed CORS origin, or an XSS in the SPA) can run arbitrary mutations as the token's OpenCTI user. That includes deleting or editing intel, importing bundles, and managing users or connectors if the token is privileged. The SPA itself sends a write mutation (stixObjectOrStixRelationshipImport), so the proxy is not read-only by design. On main (#114) the route parses each document and forwards only read queries on allowlisted root fields; mutations are refused unless OPENCTI_ALLOW_IMPORT=true, which admits only the SPA's ImportStix, and subscriptions are always refused. Evidence on main: server/src/index.js:310-342 (document checked by checkOpenCtiDocument, :255-296, before forwarding); compare server/src/index.js:344-374 (MISP read-only allowlist); src/app/services/opencti.service.ts:289-294 (SPA sends the ImportStix mutation); src/app/services/opencti.service.ts:344-346 (proxy-mode GraphQL endpoint)
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main (#114): before forwarding, the route parses the document with graphql's parser (checkOpenCtiDocument, server/src/index.js:255-296, applied at :328-331) and allowlists operations by root field (about, indicators and threatActors, extendable with OPENCTI_ALLOWED_QUERY_FIELDS, server/src/index.js:241-246) rather than by operation name or persisted query hash; root-level fragments are refused (:272-276); `mutation` documents are refused except the SPA's ImportStix selecting only stixObjectOrStixRelationshipImport, behind the separate OPENCTI_ALLOW_IMPORT flag (:247-249, :281-288), which server/.env.example:36 leaves false; subscriptions are always refused (:278-280). server/.env.example:28-33 says OPENCTI_TOKEN should belong to a least-privileged, read-mostly OpenCTI user.

threats.title: A shared origin such as teamstarwolf.github.io in the proxy's CORS allowlist lets every Pages site in the org drive the proxy
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: Because the SPA cannot send the proxy token, CORS is the only control on what browser code may drive the proxy. `server/.env.example` puts `https://teamstarwolf.github.io` in ALLOWED_ORIGINS. On GitHub Pages that origin covers every project site under the TeamStarWolf org, not just /ATTACK-Navi/. So any script served from another org repo's Pages site, or any script compromise of the hosted SPA (a malicious dependency or tampered bundled data), can call the analyst's local proxy and read the responses. That includes the OpenCTI mutation path. On main (#114) server/.env.example lists only http://localhost:4200 and warns against origins the operator does not run, and the SPA can send the proxy token. Evidence on main: server/.env.example:9-12 (ALLOWED_ORIGINS is http://localhost:4200 only); server/src/index.js:27-47 (origin-only allowlist); README.md:203 (add your own deployment origin, never a shared one); package.json:5 (homepage on the shared teamstarwolf.github.io origin)
threats.mitigation: The code default is `http://localhost:4200` (server/src/index.js:30), and an empty list fails closed (server/src/index.js:36-37). Implemented on main (#114): the github.io entry is gone from `.env.example`, which now lists only http://localhost:4200 and warns against listing origins the operator does not run (server/.env.example:9-12); README.md:203 says to add your own deployment origin, never a shared one; and the SPA sends PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN as X-Proxy-Key when the operator enters it (src/app/services/proxy-headers.ts:15-19; one token per proxy, not per user), so the token can be required. Using the hosted Pages app with the proxy would mean listing the shared origin, which README.md:203 rules out; the shared-origin exposure of the hosted app itself is tracked as 092cad7e.

threats.title: DNS rebinding can read MISP events through a loopback-bound proxy
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: The proxy never checks the Host header, and it treats requests with no Origin header as allowed. A malicious site can rebind its hostname to 127.0.0.1 and then make same-origin GET requests to http://<attacker-host>:8787/api/misp/events/view/<id> or servers/getVersion. Browsers send no Origin on same-origin GETs, so CORS allows the request. With PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN empty (as the SPA requires), the proxy adds the MISP API key and returns the event JSON to the attacker's page. The page can enumerate event IDs. POSTs, including OpenCTI, carry an Origin header and are refused. The 127.0.0.1 publish in docker-compose does not stop this, because the victim's own browser makes the requests. On main (#114) every /api route except /api/health first checks the Host name against localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 and ALLOWED_HOSTS (421 otherwise) and requires the X-Requested-With header, so a rebound page is refused before any upstream call. Evidence on main: server/src/index.js:37 (`!origin` still allowed by CORS); server/src/index.js:95 (no token check when the token is unset); server/src/index.js:348-353, 362-374, 381-389 (GET events/view/* forwarded with the MISP key, response relayed); server/src/index.js:394 (GET route); Host validation in requireAllowedHost (:113-133) and the X-Requested-With requirement in requireClientHeader (:140-145), both applied to /api at :306 of server/src/index.js
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main (#114): a request whose Host name is not localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 or listed in ALLOWED_HOSTS gets 421, with ports ignored (requireAllowedHost, server/src/index.js:113-133), and a rebound page's Host is the attacker's own name, so it is refused there; every /api route except /api/health requires X-Requested-With, so every cross-origin call needs a preflight (requireClientHeader, server/src/index.js:140-145); both run before the MISP key is attached to any upstream call (server/src/index.js:306). docker-compose sets ALLOWED_HOSTS from APP_HOST, empty by default (docker-compose.yml:41-42). PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN is usable from the SPA (X-Proxy-Key, src/app/services/proxy-headers.ts:15-19), so it can be required as well.

threats.title: A proxy caller could steer the credentialed upstream fetch to another host, traverse paths or reach MISP write endpoints
threats.description: A caller could try to steer the credentialed fetch to another host, add `..` segments, or reach MISP write endpoints such as events/add or users/add while the operator's key is attached. Evidence: server/src/index.js:201-224 (validateUpstreamUrl); server/src/index.js:317 (fixed 'graphql' path); server/src/index.js:348-374 (MISP allowlist and 403); server/src/index.js:365-366 (only the endpoint path splat, req.params.endpoint, used); src/app/services/misp.service.ts:297 (SPA's events/add, blocked by the proxy); server/test/proxy.test.js:160,344 (tests), :239-302 (traversal and non-allowlisted endpoints refused, multi-segment endpoints proxied)
threats.mitigation: `validateUpstreamUrl` takes the upstream origin from env only. It strips leading slashes, rejects `..` and `//`, limits the path to `[\w\-./]`, and checks that the resolved origin equals the configured origin. Query strings are not forwarded, because only the endpoint path splat (req.params.endpoint) is used. MISP paths must match a four-entry read-only allowlist, so the SPA's own /events/add call gets a 403. Express URL-decodes params before these checks, so encoded `%2e%2e` is still caught. Tests cover the allowlist rejection, traversal refusals (dot segments, encoded slashes, absolute paths) and forwarding only to the configured upstream.

threats.title: Proxy error responses disclose upstream fetch error text and the requested endpoint
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: A rejected CORS origin calls `callback(new Error(...))`, and malformed JSON makes express.json throw. Both fall through to Express's default finalhandler, which returns `err.stack` whenever NODE_ENV is not 'production'. Neither the proxy Dockerfile nor docker-compose sets NODE_ENV. A disallowed caller therefore gets a 500 response with server file paths and dependency versions. The upstream catch blocks also return `error.message` from fetch. The 403 response echoes the requested endpoint, though as JSON. On main (#120) a CORS denial carries status 403, a final JSON error handler answers every error without the stack, and server/Dockerfile sets NODE_ENV=production; the upstream catch still returns the fetch error message, and the 403 still echoes the endpoint. Evidence on main: server/src/index.js:40-44 (CORS Error, now with status 403, passed to next); server/src/index.js:52 (express.json; parse errors reach the JSON error handler at :405-414); server/src/index.js:191 (fetch error.message still returned; :186-189 answer size and timeout failures with fixed messages); server/src/index.js:373 (endpoint echoed); server/Dockerfile:5-7 (NODE_ENV=production); server/node_modules/finalhandler/index.js:157-162 (getErrorMessage returns err.stack when env !== 'production'; finalhandler 2.1.1 per server/package-lock.json; errors no longer reach it because the proxy's own handler answers first)
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main (#120): server/Dockerfile sets NODE_ENV=production; a final Express error handler returns JSON (the message only for 4xx, a generic message for 5xx) and logs 5xx details on the server; CORS denials still pass an Error, now with status 403, which that handler answers as JSON. Remaining: return a generic message instead of the fetch error text when an upstream call fails (server/src/index.js:191), and stop echoing the requested endpoint in the MISP 403 response (server/src/index.js:373).

threats.title: No audit log of who used the operator's credentials
threats.description: Every upstream action is attributed, in OpenCTI and MISP, to the single operator token held by the proxy. The proxy logs only a startup line, the missing-token or fail-closed warning, and 5xx errors. It records no client IP, origin, route, GraphQL operation name, or status per request. If a caller that gets through (a holder of the proxy token, a local process on a loopback bind with no token, or a script on an allowed origin) bulk-reads MISP or OpenCTI, or runs the ImportStix mutation where OPENCTI_ALLOW_IMPORT is on, nobody can say which caller did it. Evidence: server/src/index.js:69-79, 409 and 420-427 (the only logging); server/src/index.js:177-196, 333-341 and 381-389 (upstream calls with no logging)
threats.mitigation: Add per-request structured logging (timestamp, remote address, Origin, Host, route, GraphQL operationName or a hash of the query, upstream status). Never log tokens or request bodies. Consider shipping logs off the host.

threats.title: The proxy has no rate or concurrency limit on credentialed upstream calls
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: The proxy accepts JSON bodies up to 5 MB and forwards them. Upstream `fetch` calls have no AbortSignal or timeout, and `upstream.text()` buffers the whole upstream response in memory with no size cap. There is no rate limiting or concurrency limit. A caller can tie up sockets with slow upstreams, exhaust proxy memory with large MISP restSearch results, or hammer OpenCTI with expensive GraphQL queries under the operator's identity. On main (#114) the default body limit is 1 MB (MAX_BODY_SIZE), upstream calls are aborted after UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS (30 s), and an upstream body above UPSTREAM_MAX_BYTES (10 MB) is cut off with a 502; there is still no rate or concurrency limit. Evidence on main: server/src/index.js:52 (1 MB default body limit); server/src/index.js:177-196 (upstream fetch with an abort timer and the bounded read at :161-174)
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main (#114): upstream fetches carry an AbortController signal that fires after UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS, the streamed response is capped at UPSTREAM_MAX_BYTES, and the JSON limit defaults to 1 MB. Remaining: add express-rate-limit or a reverse-proxy rate limit. Consider GraphQL depth or complexity limits.

data.name: server/.env secrets file
data.description: Plaintext dotenv file on the operator's host that holds OPENCTI_URL/TOKEN, MISP_URL/API_KEY, PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN and ALLOWED_ORIGINS. It is gitignored and loaded at runtime through env_file. The root .dockerignore excludes server/ and every .env file (.dockerignore:7-14), so the root image's `COPY . .` build stage (Dockerfile:9) does not receive it, and server/.dockerignore keeps .env out of the proxy image's build context; the final nginx stage copies only dist (Dockerfile:14).

threats.title: Integration secrets sit in plaintext env, and the upstream URL scheme is not enforced
threats.description: OPENCTI_TOKEN and MISP_API_KEY live in plaintext in server/.env, and docker-compose loads them into container env, where `docker inspect` shows them. At the 5831e2d baseline the root `.dockerignore` did not exclude `server/.env`, so the root Dockerfile build stage's `COPY . .` put the secrets in the app's build-stage layer and build cache; on main (#120) the root `.dockerignore` excludes `server/` and every `.env` file, and server/.dockerignore keeps `.env` out of the proxy image's build context. The final nginx stage copies only dist. At the 5831e2d baseline the Helm chart's values.yaml and docs/HELM.md carried OPENCTI_TOKEN and MISP_API_KEY placeholders that no template read; on main (#115) the chart has no proxy values and docs/HELM.md says never to put integration secrets in values.yaml. `validateUpstreamUrl` also never checks for https, so a mistaken `http://` OPENCTI_URL or MISP_URL sends the bearer token or API key in cleartext. Node's default TLS verification is not overridden anywhere. Evidence: server/.env.example:34-41; docker-compose.yml:26-31 (env_file, optional); .dockerignore:7-14 (server/ and .env files excluded); Dockerfile:9 (COPY . .); Dockerfile:14 (final stage copies dist only); helm/attack-nav/values.yaml (no proxy block since #115); docs/HELM.md (Backend proxy section: no token values); server/src/index.js:201-224 (no protocol check); .gitignore:52
threats.mitigation: `.gitignore` excludes server/.env (.gitignore:52), and no .env is committed. Implemented on main: the root `.dockerignore` excludes `server` and `**/.env` (#120), and the chart has no plaintext token values (#115); docs/HELM.md suggests running the proxy separately with its configuration in a Kubernetes Secret. Remaining: the secrets are still plaintext in server/.env, and under docker compose they are loaded into the proxy container env, where `docker inspect` shows them (docker-compose.yml:26-31); and non-https upstream URLs should be rejected unless an explicit opt-in is set.

data.name: User's MISP server
data.description: Operator-owned MISP instance. The browser reaches it directly with the raw API key in the Authorization header, or the proxy reaches it with MISP_API_KEY. In direct mode the SPA can also POST /events/add, which writes to MISP. The proxy blocks that endpoint with its read-only allowlist.

data.name: User's OpenCTI server
data.description: Operator-owned OpenCTI GraphQL API. The browser reaches it directly with 'Authorization: Bearer <token>', or the proxy reaches it with OPENCTI_TOKEN. In direct mode the SPA chooses the GraphQL text, so whatever the token permits, including mutations, is reachable. In proxy mode the proxy forwards only read queries on allowlisted root fields, plus the SPA's ImportStix mutation when OPENCTI_ALLOW_IMPORT=true (server/src/index.js:255-296).

threats.title: CSV export of threat-intel indicators allows formula injection from OpenCTI and MISP content
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: exportIndicatorCsv writes OpenCTI indicator pattern and pattern_type values, and MISP galaxy cluster values, into CSV cells. Values only have their quotes doubled, and the type field is placed inside quotes without escaping. There is no handling of a leading = + - @ or tab/CR. Indicator content is often taken from external feeds and can be written by an adversary. A crafted pattern or pattern_type can break out of the cell or run as a spreadsheet formula (DDE or HYPERLINK exfiltration) when the analyst opens threat-intel-indicators.csv in Excel or Sheets. On main (#132) every row goes through the shared csvRow helper in src/app/utils/csv.ts, which quotes each field, doubles embedded quotes and prefixes a leading = + - @ tab or CR with a single quote. Evidence on main: src/app/components/threat-intelligence-panel/threat-intelligence-panel.component.ts:175-182 (MISP values), :187-196 (OpenCTI pattern/patternType), :212-220 (exportIndicatorCsv writes each row with csvRow); src/app/services/opencti.service.ts:238-239
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main (#132): a single CSV helper (csvCell/csvRow) quotes every field, doubles embedded quotes, and prefixes cells that start with = + - @ \t or \r with a single quote (src/app/utils/csv.ts:9, :26-37). exportIndicatorCsv writes every row through csvRow (src/app/components/threat-intelligence-panel/threat-intelligence-panel.component.ts:212-220), as do the asset, gap and roadmap exports (src/app/services/asset-inventory.service.ts:220; src/app/components/gap-view/gap-view.component.ts:265; src/app/components/roadmap-panel/roadmap-panel.component.ts:182).

data.name: User's TAXII 2.1 servers
data.description: Operator-configured TAXII 2.1 servers. The SPA does discovery at <url>/taxii2/, then calls whichever api_roots the server returns, sending the same HTTP Basic credentials there. A server-supplied api_root on another host therefore receives the analyst's Basic credentials. Fetched collection bundles are imported into the local STIX collection.

data.name: Static hosting tier
data.description: Where the built SPA and bundled data are served: GitHub Pages, built by GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/deploy.yml), or the nginx Docker image deployed through docker-compose or the Helm chart (Dockerfile:12-28, helm/attack-nav/templates/deployment.yaml). Bundled data enters through the PR-reviewed monthly refresh workflow (.github/workflows/refresh-data.yml).

data.name: nginx static server (Docker / Helm)
data.description: Self-hosted alternative: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged serving the production build on port 8080 as the unprivileged user 101 (Dockerfile:12-14, :27), with an SPA fallback, security headers and a same-origin /api/ route to the optional proxy (nginx.conf:10-45). nginx.conf and nginx-security-headers.conf are templates that the image's entrypoint renders into /etc/nginx/conf.d at container start (Dockerfile:15-19). The CSP connect-src allows 'self', a fixed set of public hosts and whatever CSP_EXTRA_CONNECT_SRC adds (nginx-security-headers.conf:14), so proxy mode through /api/ works under the CSP, while direct-mode MISP, OpenCTI or TAXII hosts must be added through CSP_EXTRA_CONNECT_SRC. docker-compose publishes it as 8080:8080 on all interfaces (docker-compose.yml:4-5). The Helm chart runs only this container, as non-root with a read-only root filesystem and emptyDir volumes at /tmp and /etc/nginx/conf.d (helm/attack-nav/values.yaml:43-58; helm/attack-nav/templates/deployment.yaml:16-24, :40-55). It has no proxy values or template (helm/attack-nav/values.yaml:60-62), so its /api/ route points at the image default http://proxy:8787 (Dockerfile:24-26; nginx.conf:36-38), which the chart does not deploy, so /api/ requests fail (502, nginx.conf:30-31), and TLS is left to an optional Ingress (helm/attack-nav/values.yaml:25-33).

threats.title: The Helm chart points at an image no workflow publishes, and images and base images are referenced by mutable tags
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: The chart's default image ghcr.io/teamstarwolf/attack-nav:latest, and the proxy image, are not published by any workflow here: docker.yml builds and smoke-tests but never pushes, with contents: read only. Users therefore pull whatever was last pushed by hand to that namespace, under a mutable `latest` tag with `pullPolicy: IfNotPresent`. Nodes may keep running different, unverifiable builds. The base images are unpinned (`nginx:alpine`) or end-of-life (`node:20-alpine` for the proxy; Node 20 reached EOL in April 2026, and proxy CI still tests on Node 20). Dependabot has no docker ecosystem entry. The Deployment sets no securityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, dropped capabilities), so nginx runs as root, and the proxy Dockerfile has no USER. The `proxy` values block is read by no template, even though docs/HELM.md describes a sidecar. On main, #115 moved the app image to nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged on 8080, added a pod and container securityContext, defaulted the tag to the chart's appVersion and removed the proxy block, and #120 moved the proxy image to node:24-alpine with USER node and added docker ecosystems to Dependabot. Still open: no workflow publishes either image, base images are referenced by tag rather than digest, and pullPolicy is IfNotPresent. Evidence on main: helm/attack-nav/values.yaml:3-14 (tag defaults to appVersion, IfNotPresent); helm/attack-nav/templates/deployment.yaml:16-24 (pod and container securityContext; one container); .github/workflows/docker.yml:37-38,52-53 (contents: read; build only, no push); Dockerfile:13 (nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:alpine, tag only); server/Dockerfile:3 (node:24-alpine; USER node at :19); .github/workflows/proxy-tests.yml:29 (Node 24); .github/dependabot.yml:25-38 (docker ecosystems for / and /server); README.md:226 (no workflow publishes an image; the chart has no proxy template or values); docs/HELM.md:150-152 (publishing images is an owner decision not yet made)
threats.mitigation: Publish signed images from CI with provenance (e.g. a docker/build-push-action pinned to a SHA, cosign or attestations). Reference images by version tag plus digest. Pin base images by digest. Implemented on main: the proxy runs node:24-alpine with `USER node` and dependabot.yml has `docker` ecosystems (#120); the chart sets a pod and container securityContext (nginx-unprivileged on 8080, readOnlyRootFilesystem, with /tmp and /etc/nginx/conf.d as emptyDir volumes), and the proxy values block and the docs claim are gone (#115).

data.name: Bundled static assets (dist / src/assets/data)
data.description: The build output: app JS and CSS, plus bundled ATT&CK enterprise, ICS and mobile and CTID F3 STIX snapshots and mapping JSON, served same-origin from Pages or nginx. Used for first paint and as a fallback when the live fetch fails. A scheduled CI workflow refreshes the snapshots monthly with curl from raw.githubusercontent.com, does a shape check, and opens a PR for human review before deploy.

threats.title: The monthly data refresh takes unverified upstream branch heads into a PR too large to review
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: refresh-data.yml downloads ATT&CK STIX from the mitre-attack/attack-stix-data `master` branch, the CTID F3 bundle from `main`, and CVE2CAPEC data from Galeax/CVE2CAPEC `main`. It checks no commit pin, hash or signature, only a structural check (type=bundle and an object count). The resulting PR rewrites src/assets/data/enterprise-attack.json (about 53 MB) and other JSON that no reviewer can read meaningfully. The PR is opened with GITHUB_TOKEN, which does not trigger pull_request workflows, and no workflow runs unit tests on PRs anyway. So the PR body's claim that 'CI (unit tests + build) validates the parse' is false. Once merged, deploy.yml ships the data to every user. A compromised or mistaken upstream commit can silently change technique, mitigation or CVE mappings that analysts rely on. Markup-based XSS is limited because AttackTextPipe reduces descriptions to plain text. On main (#116, #139) the workflow resolves the current commit of the attack-stix-data and F3 branches and downloads at that SHA (recorded in the PR), gates the bundles with scripts/check-refreshed-bundles.mjs (shape, object floor, no version downgrade), runs the unit suite and the production build against the refreshed data before the PR is opened, holds write permissions only in the open-pr job, and ci.yml runs unit tests on pull requests. Still open: the pinned commit is whatever the upstream branch head is at run time, with no publisher checksum or signature; CVE2CAPEC is still fetched from Galeax `main`; the data diff is still not human-readable. Evidence on main: .github/workflows/refresh-data.yml:26-27 (workflow-level read; write only in the open-pr job at :156-158); .github/workflows/refresh-data.yml:48-84 (branch head resolved, downloads at that SHA, bundle gate); .github/workflows/refresh-data.yml:86-87 and scripts/build-cve-technique-map.mjs:31,140 (Galeax main fetch); .github/workflows/refresh-data.yml:199-201 and 245-250 (workflow-token PR; body cites the tests and build that ran); README.md:211 (ci.yml runs unit tests on every pull request); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:4-5,36-39 (merge to main deploys); src/app/pipes/attack-text.pipe.ts:5-16 (rendering limits XSS)
threats.mitigation: Implemented on main: each run downloads at the upstream commit it resolved and records it, the PR body carries a per-bundle version and object-count table, ci.yml runs `ng test` and a production build on pull_request (the workflow-token PR needs `gh workflow run ci.yml` to get that check), and `contents: write` is scoped to the open-pr job. Remaining: pin each source to a reviewed release tag and verify checksums, pin the Galeax source, produce a human-readable semantic diff (objects added, removed or changed, and their IDs) in the PR body, and open the PR with a GitHub App or PAT token so CI runs on it.

data.name: GitHub Pages host
data.description: Default public hosting (https://teamstarwolf.github.io/ATTACK-Navi/). CI builds the SPA and deploy-pages publishes it. Pages cannot set response headers and index.html has no CSP meta tag, so the hosted site runs with no Content-Security-Policy. The origin https://teamstarwolf.github.io is shared by every TeamStarWolf project page, and README.md:203 tells proxy operators never to list a shared origin in ALLOWED_ORIGINS.

threats.title: GitHub Pages deployment ships without any CSP, Trusted Types or framing protection
threats.description: The hosted build (deploy.yml builds with --base-href /ATTACK-Navi/ and uploads dist to Pages) serves src/index.html, which has no <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">. GitHub Pages cannot set response headers, so the only CSP in the repo (nginx-security-headers.conf, included by nginx.conf) never reaches Pages users. There is also no require-trusted-types-for and no framing control. If any script injection succeeds on the hosted site, nothing limits it. It can read the in-memory OpenCTI token and MISP key used in direct mode, TAXII Basic credentials, the NVD key in sessionStorage, and all localStorage and IndexedDB work product, and it can send them to any origin. The page also pulls a third-party stylesheet from fonts.googleapis.com without SRI. Google Fonts are also loaded from fonts.googleapis.com without Subresource Integrity. Evidence: src/index.html:1-19 (no CSP meta; Google Fonts link at :7-8); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:36-39; nginx-security-headers.conf:14 (CSP exists only for the nginx image); README.md:222; src/index.html:1-19 (no CSP meta; line 8 Google Fonts stylesheet); angular.json:50,66 (service worker and hashing configured, no CSP option); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:36-39,52-53 (dist deployed to Pages as-is); README.md:182-183 (tokens kept in browser memory in direct mode)
threats.mitigation: Add a meta CSP to src/index.html: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; a connect-src allowlist covering only the upstream hosts actually fetched; require-trusted-types-for 'script'. frame-ancestors cannot be set by meta, so document that the Pages site can be framed, or use the nginx/Helm deployment for credentialed use. The attackText pipe (src/app/pipes/attack-text.pipe.ts:18-56) reduces the injection surface, but it is not a CSP.

threats.title: The Pages build job runs dependency install scripts, and its artifact is deployed as-is
threats.description: At the 5831e2d baseline: deploy.yml grants `pages: write` and `id-token: write` at workflow level, so the build job gets them too. That job runs `npm ci` (install scripts from roughly 500 packages), Karma tests and the Angular build, then uploads the artifact that deploy-pages publishes as-is. A malicious dependency in that job can already alter the shipped bundle, and also holds OIDC and Pages-write scope it does not need. The deploy runs on every push to main and daily on a schedule. First-party actions (actions/checkout@v7, setup-node@v7, upload-pages-artifact@v5, deploy-pages@v5) are pinned to mutable major tags. e2e.yml uses v6 tags. On main (#119) the workflow-level token is contents: read, only the deploy job holds `pages: write` and `id-token: write`, and the actions in every workflow are pinned to commit SHAs; the build job still runs `npm ci` with lifecycle scripts. Evidence on main: .github/workflows/deploy.yml:10-14 (workflow-level contents: read only); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:21-39 (build job: contents: read; npm ci, tests, build, upload); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:41-53 (deploy job holds pages and id-token write); .github/workflows/deploy.yml:4-8 (push, daily schedule, dispatch); .github/workflows/e2e.yml:54-55 (SHA-pinned checkout and setup-node); .github/workflows/osv-scanner.yml:42,51 (SHA pins)
threats.mitigation: Partial: the only third-party actions (google/osv-scanner-action reusable workflows) are pinned to commit SHAs (.github/workflows/osv-scanner.yml:42,51). Dependabot updates github-actions (.github/dependabot.yml:18-23). The other workflows use contents: read (.github/workflows/docker.yml:37-38, .github/workflows/e2e.yml:42-43, .github/workflows/proxy-tests.yml:16-17). Implemented on main (#119): `pages: write` and `id-token: write` are on the deploy job only, the build job has `contents: read`, and first-party actions are pinned to SHAs too. Remaining: the build job still runs `npm ci` with lifecycle scripts (.github/workflows/deploy.yml:31), and the artifact it uploads is published as-is (.github/workflows/deploy.yml:37-39, :52-53); use `npm ci --ignore-scripts` where the build allows it.

data.name: Public internet
data.description: Untrusted transport and third-party publishers: raw.githubusercontent.com, api.github.com, gitlab.com, Google Fonts, NVD, FIRST, CISA, and any MISP, OpenCTI or TAXII server exposed publicly. Content crossing this boundary is parsed by the SPA, cached in IndexedDB and the SW cache, and trusted without signatures.

data.name: Upstream data publishers
data.description: Public content hosts the SPA fetches at runtime with no integrity check beyond JSON parsing: MITRE ATT&CK STIX and CTID F3 on raw.githubusercontent.com, the MISP galaxy, CTID/Sigma/Elastic/Splunk/Red Canary content, api.github.com tree listings, the ExploitDB CSV on gitlab.com, the ATT&CK releases API, and Google Fonts.

threats.title: Live ATT&CK and community data come from mutable branches with no integrity check, and are cached as authoritative
threats.description: The default data mode is 'live'. The ATT&CK and F3 STIX bundles are fetched from the moving master/main branches of raw.githubusercontent.com. Each bundle is saved to IndexedDB for 24 hours and to the service worker's attack-stix data group, and it replaces the bundled snapshot. That snapshot is the only data that gets human review, through the refresh-data PR. There is no hash, signature or schema check on the live payload. About 30 other runtime sources also track mutable branches, including personal repositories: mukul975/Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills, mdecrevoisier/SIGMA-detection-rules (rule content analysts copy into SIEMs), and stamparm/ipsum (IOC blocklist). A compromised or force-pushed upstream, or a poisoned cache, can quietly change coverage scores, detections, mitigations and URLs. Reference URLs from this data reach [href] bindings and the generated HTML report only as http(s) URLs (#132: src/app/services/data.service.ts:949-968; src/app/services/html-report.service.ts:34-42), so a tampered bundle cannot plant a script link that way. Evidence: src/app/services/data.service.ts:23-51 (master/main liveUrls), :81 (mode='live'), :273-278 (live fetch -> saveToIDB, no validation), :316 (24h TTL), :324-330; ngsw-config.json:30-38; .github/workflows/refresh-data.yml:64-84,199-280; src/app/services/anthropic-skills.service.ts:18-19,40; src/app/services/sigma.service.ts:174,274; src/app/services/ioc-feed.service.ts:37
threats.mitigation: Pin live URLs to release tags or commit SHAs and check a SHA-256 published alongside the build. Alternatively, make the reviewed bundled snapshot the default and treat live mode as opt-in, with a visible freshness and source indicator. Validate STIX shape and URL schemes before caching to IndexedDB. For community and personal sources, show provenance in the UI and allow them to be disabled.
